l: Thebes, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter THESEUS]
s: Thebes is the place to which Oedipus's sons would take him back, although he refuses to return. Oedipus's corpse is prophesied to threaten the welfare of Thebes if it becomes hostile to the land sheltering him.

l: Apollo’s oracle, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter THESEUS]
s: The oracle has warned Oedipus's sons that destruction awaits them in the land where Oedipus is received.

l: Oedipus's corpse, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter THESEUS]
s: Oedipus offers his corpse to the land that shelters him. Once buried, it will drink the warm life-blood of his enemies and become a source of power against those who threaten that land, if Zeus and Phoebus remain true.

l: Oedipus's exile, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter THESEUS]
s: Oedipus says that his own flesh and blood expelled him from his country and that he can never return there as a parricide. Theseus treats his continued banishment as acceptable and offers him a secure place in the land under his protection.

l: Oedipus's death and burial, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter THESEUS]
s: Oedipus says that the benefit he offers will be realized when he is dead and Theseus has buried him. He presents this final service as the guarantee of all the benefits his presence will bring.

l: Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter CREON with attendants]
s: Creon comes from Thebes to persuade Oedipus to return, claiming that the Thebans and especially Creon mourn his suffering. Oedipus rejects Creon's offer, accusing him of seeking to place Oedipus on Thebes' borders rather than bring him home, and Creon orders his guards to seize Antigone and Oedipus's other daughter. The Chorus of Colonus resists, and Theseus arrives, orders the maidens rescued, and threatens to hold Creon accountable under Athenian law. Oedipus defends himself against Creon's accusations of parricide and incest, insisting that he acted unknowingly and under divine compulsion.

l: Oedipus, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter CREON with attendants]
s: Oedipus refuses Creon's request that he return to Thebes and accuses him of disguising hostile intentions in soft words. When Creon seizes his daughters, Oedipus appeals to the people of Athens and curses Creon, then defends himself by arguing that his parricide and incest were committed unknowingly and through the gods' design.

l: Creon, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter CREON with attendants]
s: Creon comes as a representative of Thebes, claiming that he mourns Oedipus and wants him to return home. After Oedipus refuses, Creon has Antigone seized and threatens to take Oedipus's other daughter and Oedipus himself; Theseus condemns his actions and orders him to restore the maidens.

l: Theseus, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter CREON with attendants]
s: Theseus arrives after hearing the outcry and orders his men to pursue and rescue Oedipus's daughters. He declares that Creon has violated the laws and customs of Athens and insists that nothing short of Theseus's death will prevent him from restoring the maidens.

l: Antigone, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter CREON with attendants]
s: Antigone is seized by Creon's guards and dragged away by force. She calls for help and tells Oedipus that the guards will not let her reach him.

l: Oedipus's other daughter, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter CREON with attendants]
s: Creon states that Oedipus's other daughter has also been seized or will soon be carried off. Theseus orders that she and Antigone be rescued.

l: Creon's guards, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter CREON with attendants]
s: Creon's guards carry out his order to seize Antigone and drag her away despite her resistance. They are pursued by Theseus's men before they can take the maidens home.

l: the Chorus, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter CREON with attendants]
s: The Chorus of Colonus rejects Creon's seizure of the maidens, calls him a wrongdoer, and threatens to fight if he does not release them. It calls the people to rally and defend the State, then supports Oedipus and welcomes Theseus's intervention.

l: the Athenian people, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter CREON with attendants]
s: The Athenian people are invoked by Oedipus and the Chorus to defend the maidens and the State. Creon claims that he did not think Athens was without men or counsel, while Theseus acts in their name to enforce its laws.

l: the Theban commons, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter CREON with attendants]
s: Creon says that the Thebans claim Oedipus back and that he has mourned Oedipus's misfortunes as his kinsman. Oedipus accuses Creon of acting for Thebes's advantage rather than out of genuine welcome.

l: Thebes, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter CREON with attendants]
s: Thebes is described by Creon as Oedipus's old foster-mother and the place that seeks his return. Theseus warns Creon that his conduct shames both Thebes and his own country, and Creon threatens war with Thebes if he is touched or harmed.

l: Athens, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter CREON with attendants]
s: Athens is presented as a State that protects suppliants, champions right, and requires actions to be justified by law. Theseus acts to prevent Creon from carrying away Oedipus's daughters and declares that Athens will not tolerate such conduct.

l: Colonus, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter CREON with attendants]
s: Colonus is identified as the place where the Chorus and its people defend Oedipus and his daughters. Theseus is called away from the altar of Poseidon, lord of Colonus, to respond to the abduction.

l: Oedipus's exile, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter CREON with attendants]
s: Oedipus recalls that he once sought exile as a release, but says that Creon refused him then and later expelled him from his country. Creon now urges him to return to Thebes, while Oedipus chooses to remain where he is under the protection of Athens.

l: the abduction of Oedipus's daughters, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter CREON with attendants]
s: Creon orders his guards to take Antigone and Oedipus's other daughter after Oedipus refuses to return to Thebes. The Chorus resists the abduction, and Theseus orders his men to pursue the captors and restore the maidens.

l: the threatened conflict between Athens and Thebes, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter CREON with attendants]
s: Creon threatens that touching or harming him will mean war with Thebes. Theseus refuses to yield and says that Creon's actions will be answered under the laws of Athens.

l: Athenian law and justice, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter CREON with attendants]
s: Theseus declares that Athenian laws will adjudicate Creon's conduct and condemns him for acting like a freebooter in a State governed by law. Creon claims that he believed Justice in Athens would not permit a parricide and incestuous outcast to remain within its borders.

l: Oedipus's parricide and incest, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter CREON with attendants]
s: Creon calls Oedipus a godless parricide and reproaches him for incestuous marriage ties. Oedipus answers that he unknowingly killed his father and unknowingly married his mother, arguing that he should not be blamed for acts committed without knowledge and under the gods' compulsion.

l: Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus longs to witness the battle in which Theseus and his warriors confront the flying foe and rescue the two captive maidens. It imagines the conflict near Pythian shore, the torch-lit bay, or the glen west of white Oea. The Chorus calls on Zeus, Athene, Apollo, and the Huntress to help Athens and bring victory. At the end, an escort is said to be approaching with the maidens.

l: Chorus, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: The Chorus hopes to witness the battle and hear its roar. It prays to Zeus, Athene, Apollo, and the Huntress for aid, and longs to see the captive maidens rescued.

l: flying foe, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: The flying foe is expected to turn at last to bay and give blow for blow. It is approaching the glen west of white Oea’s scaur and is expected to be vanquished.

l: battle, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: The battle is imagined near the Pythian shore, the torch-lit bay, or the glen west of white Oea. The Chorus longs to see and hear the fray from above.

l: Theseus, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: Theseus is identified as the bold captain and chieftain whose men confront the robber band. He is expected to rescue the two captive maidens by force.

l: Antigone, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: The two maidens are captives who have been badly treated and buffeted by their kin. An escort is said to be drawing near with them.

l: captivity of the maidens, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: The maidens’ captivity results from their seizure by a robber band. Theseus is expected to rescue them before the band flees the land.

l: Theseus's warriors, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: Theseus’s warriors are described as dreadful and are expected to vanquish the flying foes. They charge as gallant knights with flashing bridles.

l: Pallas, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: Pallas is named as a patron adored by the warriors.

l: victory, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: Victory is expected to come on this day. The Chorus believes that Zeus is working some great thing to bring it about.

l: Zeus, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: Zeus is called all-seeing and lord of heaven. The Chorus asks him to give the guardian host strength to surprise the fleeing foes and win their prize.

l: guardian host, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: The guardian host is asked to receive triumphant might from Zeus. It is expected to surprise the flying foes and win their prize.

l: Athene, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: Athene is invoked as the undefiled child of Zeus. The Chorus asks her to hear its prayer and help Athens in its hour of danger.

l: Athens, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: Athens is described as being in danger. The Chorus asks divine powers to help it through that danger.

l: escort, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, CHORUS.
s: An escort is reported to be drawing near with the maidens. Its approach is presented as confirming that the watchers will not be misled by false presage.

l: Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE with THESEUS]
s: Antigone and Ismene are brought back safely to Oedipus by Theseus, who has fulfilled his promise. Polyneices comes as a suppliant, explains his claim against Eteocles and his expedition against Thebes, and asks Oedipus for support, but Oedipus curses both sons. Polyneices refuses Antigone’s plea to turn back and asks that he and his allies receive burial if he dies. Thunder and lightning announce Oedipus’s approaching death; he calls Theseus, promises him a secret that will protect the land, and is led toward the place where he will die.

l: Oedipus, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE with THESEUS]
s: Oedipus welcomes Antigone and Ismene after Theseus brings them back safely, and he thanks Theseus for their rescue. He refuses to receive Polyneices favorably, condemns him for having driven him into exile, and curses Polyneices and Eteocles. When thunder and lightning signal his appointed end, he asks for Theseus and prepares to lead him to the place of his death.

l: Antigone, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE with THESEUS]
s: Antigone returns safely with Ismene under Theseus’s protection and embraces Oedipus. She persuades Oedipus to hear Polyneices and later begs Polyneices to turn his army back from Thebes. She mourns his decision to continue toward the battle and promises, at his request, to provide burial rites if he dies.

l: Ismene, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE with THESEUS]
s: Ismene is brought back safely to Oedipus by Theseus and remains with Oedipus and Antigone as Polyneices speaks. She accompanies Antigone and Theseus when they follow Oedipus toward the place appointed for his death.

l: Theseus, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE with THESEUS]
s: Theseus returns Antigone and Ismene alive and unharmed, as he had promised Oedipus. He permits Polyneices, who has taken sanctuary at Poseidon’s altar, to speak and assures Oedipus that his life is safe while Theseus lives. At Oedipus’s summons, he comes during the thunderstorm and is chosen to learn and guard the secret of Oedipus’s burial place.

l: Polyneices, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE with THESEUS]
s: Polyneices comes from Argos as a suppliant after being expelled from his native land. He says that Eteocles deprived him of the sovereign throne and that he has brought an Argive army against Thebes to recover it. Oedipus rejects him and curses him, and Polyneices nevertheless refuses to turn back, asking Antigone and Ismene to ensure his burial if he dies.

l: Eteocles, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE with THESEUS]
s: Eteocles, Polyneices’ younger brother, is said to have ousted Polyneices from the throne and to rule Thebes. Oedipus curses Eteocles and Polyneices, predicting that they will die by one another’s hands.

l: Argos, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE with THESEUS]
s: Argos is the land to which Polyneices was banished and where he married Adrastus’ child. From Argos he gathers allies and leads an army against Thebes.

l: Thebes, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE with THESEUS]
s: Thebes is ruled by Eteocles and is besieged by Polyneices and the sevenfold Argive host. Oedipus declares that Polyneices cannot storm the city before he and Eteocles become involved in mutual bloodshed.

l: Athens, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE with THESEUS]
s: Theseus is called the Athenian prince, and Oedipus speaks of the protection and welfare of Theseus’s land. Oedipus promises that the secret of his death will help preserve that land from its enemies.

l: Polyneices’ expedition against Thebes, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE with THESEUS]
s: Polyneices says that he assembled seven foremost captains and their forces in Argos to attack Thebes and recover the throne from Eteocles. He acknowledges that the expedition may end in his ruin but refuses to withdraw after his army has seen him lead it.

l: Oedipus's exile, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE with THESEUS]
s: Oedipus recalls that Polyneices drove him from his sovereignty and made him an exile without a city. He says that he has since lived in a foreign land begging for bread, aided by Antigone and Ismene.

l: Oedipus’s curse on his sons, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE with THESEUS]
s: Oedipus curses Polyneices and Eteocles, calling on Justice, Tartarus, the dread goddesses, and Ares. He declares that Polyneices will neither win Thebes nor return to Argos, and that he and Eteocles will die by one another’s hands.

l: Oedipus’s prophesied final resting-place, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE with THESEUS]
s: Oedipus interprets the repeated thunder and lightning as divine signs that his appointed end has come. He tells Theseus that he will soon die and sets out toward the place where he is to enter Hades.

l: Oedipus’s secret burial place, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE with THESEUS]
s: Oedipus tells Theseus that he will lead him to a place where he must end his life. He orders Theseus to keep the place and its location secret from everyone except his chosen heir, saying that the secret will protect Theseus and his land.

l: the thunderstorm, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE with THESEUS]
s: Thunder and lightning repeatedly intensify while Polyneices departs and Oedipus announces his approaching death. The storm is treated as a sign from Zeus and as a warning that the gods’ appointed events are being fulfilled.

l: Oedipus's daughters, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE with THESEUS]
s: Antigone and Ismene return safely and are described by Oedipus as the children who have cared for and preserved him. They accompany him toward his final destination, although he ultimately asks them not to touch or guide him.

l: Argive force, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE with THESEUS]
s: The Argive host consists of seven forces led by Polyneices and captains including Amphiaraiis, Tydeus, Eteoclus, Hippomedon, Capaneus, and Parthenopaeus. It surrounds the plain around Thebes, and Polyneices says he cannot turn it back without shame.

l: filial duty, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE with THESEUS]
s: Antigone and Ismene are praised for tending and preserving Oedipus, while Oedipus condemns Polyneices and Eteocles for failing to honor their father. Polyneices asks his sisters to complete their filial care by giving him burial if he dies.

l: death and mortality, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE with THESEUS]
s: The Chorus declares that excessive length of life brings more burdens and that death finally releases everyone from life’s troubles. Oedipus accepts that his death is appointed, while Polyneices recognizes that his expedition may lead him to death.

l: the burial of Polyneices, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE with THESEUS]
s: Polyneices asks Antigone and Ismene to grant him burial and proper funeral rites if he dies in the expedition against Thebes. He says that their care in death will add to the praise they have earned by serving their father.

l: Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter MESSENGER]
s: The Messenger reports that Oedipus has died in a mysterious, painless manner near the sacred threshold, after entrusting his daughters to Theseus. Oedipus disappears from sight while only Theseus remains to witness what happens, and the exact manner of his death is known only to Theseus. Antigone and Ismene mourn him and wish to see his burial place, but Theseus tells them that Oedipus forbade anyone to approach the hidden tomb. Theseus promises to care for the daughters, and they decide to return to Thebes to try to end the feud between their brothers.

l: Oedipus, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter MESSENGER]
s: Oedipus reaches a sacred place, prepares himself with water and offerings, and tells Antigone and Ismene that he will die that day. He entrusts them to Theseus, then orders them to leave before his final passage. He is taken from sight without wailing, disease, or pain.

l: Antigone, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter MESSENGER]
s: Antigone mourns Oedipus and recalls the loving labor of guiding his blind feet. She wishes to see his burial place, but Theseus tells her that Oedipus forbade anyone to approach it. She accepts this and proposes returning to Thebes to try to stop the conflict between her brothers.

l: Ismene, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter MESSENGER]
s: Ismene grieves Oedipus's death and wishes that she could share his fate rather than live desolate. She tells Antigone that Oedipus died without a tomb or anyone nearby, and she fears how they will continue friendless and helpless.

l: Theseus, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter MESSENGER]
s: Theseus comes to Oedipus when summoned and promises to remain a constant friend to Antigone and Ismene. He is the only person who stays to witness what happens to Oedipus and later refuses the daughters' request to see the tomb. He pledges to care for their needs and to work for their safety.

l: the Messenger, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter MESSENGER]
s: The Messenger tells the Chorus that Oedipus has passed from life to death. He describes Oedipus's final preparations, his farewell to his daughters, and his disappearance, while acknowledging that only Theseus knows exactly how Oedipus met his end.

l: the Chorus, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter MESSENGER]
s: The Chorus questions the Messenger about Oedipus's death and later comforts Antigone and Ismene. It urges them to accept their fate and assures them that refuge and safety have been found.

l: Oedipus's daughters, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter MESSENGER]
s: Oedipus's daughters, Antigone and Ismene, mourn their father's death after having cared for and guided him. Before dying, Oedipus entrusts them to Theseus, who promises not to forsake them. They later decide to return to Thebes.

l: Oedipus’s prophesied final resting-place, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter MESSENGER]
s: Oedipus's death occurs after a divine summons and is described as painless and without wailing, disease, fire, or a whirlwind. He is taken away by an unseen power, possibly a messenger from heaven or a gentle opening of the earth. Only Theseus knows the exact manner of his death.

l: Oedipus's disappearance, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter MESSENGER]
s: After Oedipus sends his daughters away, the witnesses look back and find that he has vanished from sight. They see only Theseus, who raises his hand as though shielding his eyes from an unbearable sight and then prays to Earth and Heaven.

l: the promise to protect Oedipus's daughters, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter MESSENGER]
s: Oedipus asks Theseus to take responsibility for Antigone and Ismene and never forsake them. Theseus gives his word and later promises to attend to all their needs with continued effort and care.

l: Oedipus’s secret burial place, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter MESSENGER]
s: Oedipus's tomb is a hidden, sacred burial place that Antigone and Ismene are forbidden to approach. Theseus refuses to lead them there because he promised Oedipus that no one would come near it or perform funeral rites.

l: Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, ANTIGONE
s: Antigone tells Ismene that Creon has ordered Polyneices to remain unburied and resolves to bury him despite the death penalty. Ismene refuses to help, arguing that they are women who must obey the stronger ruler, while Antigone invokes the eternal laws of Heaven. Creon announces that Eteocles will receive heroic burial but Polyneices will be left as carrion, and he threatens the guards when Polyneices’ corpse is found covered with dust. The Chorus praises humanity’s accomplishments while warning that civic and divine laws must be respected, then sees Antigone being brought before the king.

l: Antigone, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, ANTIGONE
s: Antigone resolves to bury her brother Polyneices despite Creon’s prohibition and asks Ismene to help. She rejects Ismene’s refusal, declares that she will act alone, and accepts the possibility of an honorable death in obedience to the eternal laws of Heaven.

l: Ismene, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, ANTIGONE
s: Ismene refuses to help bury Polyneices, arguing that they are weak women who must obey the ruler. She agrees to keep Antigone’s plan secret but fears that Antigone is doomed to fail.

l: Creon, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, ANTIGONE
s: Creon claims the throne after Eteocles and Polyneices die and declares that the state must come before private friendship. He orders Eteocles to receive burial honors and Polyneices to remain unburied, threatens death for anyone who disobeys, and accuses the guards of taking bribes when Polyneices’ corpse is covered with dust.

l: Polyneices, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, ANTIGONE
s: Polyneices is described as an exile who attacked his father’s city and sought to destroy Thebes. Creon therefore declares that he must receive no burial or mourning, although Antigone insists that he remains her brother.

l: Eteocles, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, ANTIGONE
s: Eteocles fought and fell in battle for his country. Creon orders that he be buried with the ceremonies and honors owed to a heroic dead man.

l: Oedipus, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, ANTIGONE
s: Oedipus is identified as the father of Antigone, Ismene, Polyneices, and Eteocles. Antigone and Ismene recall his dishonor, self-inflicted blindness, and death after he recognized his sin.

l: Zeus, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, ANTIGONE
s: Zeus is invoked as a witness to Creon’s policy of putting the state first. The Chorus says that Zeus struck the invading Argive host with lightning because of its boastfulness and impiety.

l: Chorus, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, ANTIGONE
s: The Theban elders form the Chorus and are summoned by Creon as trusted counselors. They acknowledge Creon’s authority, question their responsibility for enforcing his order, and sing of the Argive invasion and the limits imposed by law.

l: Thebes, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, ANTIGONE
s: Thebes has survived the Argive attack and celebrates the invaders’ defeat. It is described as a seven-gated city whose defenses resisted the assault.

l: Argive force, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, ANTIGONE
s: The Argive force attacks Thebes with spearmen and seven captains at the city’s seven gates. It is driven back after Zeus strikes the invading host with lightning, and the two brothers Eteocles and Polyneices die fighting each other.

l: the Guard, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, ANTIGONE
s: The Watchman reports that Polyneices’ corpse has been covered with dust and given the proper ritual, though no burial has been completed. He denies committing or witnessing the act and fears Creon’s punishment.

l: the State, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, ANTIGONE
s: Creon compares Thebes’ state to a storm-tossed ship that has reached safety. He says that loyalty to the state must take precedence over friendship and uses this principle to justify his treatment of Polyneices.

l: the royal edict, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, ANTIGONE
s: The royal edict orders that Polyneices receive no burial or mourning and that his corpse be left for dogs and birds. Anyone who violates the order is to be put to death.

l: the burial of Polyneices, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, ANTIGONE
s: The burial of Polyneices is forbidden by Creon but undertaken in part when someone sprinkles dust over the corpse and performs the proper ritual. Antigone claims that she will complete the burial despite the danger.

l: Polyneices, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, ANTIGONE
s: Polyneices’ corpse is left exposed under Creon’s order, intended to become food for dogs and carrion birds. The guards later find it covered with dust, with no visible trace of the person who performed the ritual.

l: the fratricide, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, ANTIGONE
s: The fratricide occurs when Eteocles and Polyneices kill each other in battle on the same day. The Chorus describes the brothers as the only two of the seven opposing champions who do not leave their armor behind as trophies.

l: Polyneices’ expedition against Thebes, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, ANTIGONE
s: The Argive invasion seeks to vindicate Polyneices’ claim and threatens Thebes’ walls and gates. The invasion fails when the Argive force is routed, and the city prepares to celebrate its victory.

l: death penalty, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, ANTIGONE
s: The death penalty is imposed by Creon on anyone who buries Polyneices or disobeys the royal edict. Creon also threatens the guards with death if they do not find the person responsible.

l: divine law, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, ANTIGONE
s: Divine law is represented by the eternal laws of Heaven that Antigone says she must obey over Creon’s command. The Chorus likewise warns that a person must honor both the laws of the land and the gods.

l: Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter GUARD bringing ANTIGONE]
s: The Guard brings Antigone before Creon after catching her burying the corpse in defiance of Creon’s interdict. Antigone admits the deed and says that the unwritten laws of Heaven, not Creon’s human law, required her to bury her dead brother. Creon condemns Antigone to death and also treats Ismene as guilty, though Antigone denies that Ismene helped her. Ismene tries to share Antigone’s fate, while the Chorus reflects on the inherited suffering of the Labdacidae and announces Haemon’s angry arrival.

l: Antigone, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter GUARD bringing ANTIGONE]
s: Antigone is brought before Creon after being caught burying the corpse. She openly admits the deed and defends it by appealing to the unwritten laws of Heaven, saying that she chose to die rather than leave her dead brother unburied. Creon condemns her to death, and she rejects Ismene’s attempt to share her guilt.

l: Creon, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter GUARD bringing ANTIGONE]
s: Creon questions the Guard and Antigone about the burial and insists that his interdict must be obeyed. He declares that Antigone’s defiance and pride deserve the utmost penalty, condemns her to death, and orders the guards to take both Antigone and Ismene away. He also refuses to spare Antigone because she is his sister’s child or because she is Haemon’s bride.

l: the Guard, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter GUARD bringing ANTIGONE]
s: The Guard brings Antigone to Creon after finding her burying the corpse. He recounts how the guards uncovered the body, watched through the night, saw Antigone scatter dust and pour burial rites, and then seized her. He is relieved to have escaped Creon’s anger but says that bringing disaster to a friend is grievous.

l: Ismene, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter GUARD bringing ANTIGONE]
s: Ismene appears grieving after Antigone’s arrest and claims that she took part in the deed so that she can share Antigone’s guilt. Antigone denies that Ismene helped her and refuses to let her die for an act she did not perform. Ismene says that life would have no profit without her sister and reveals that Antigone is Haemon’s plighted bride.

l: Haemon, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter GUARD bringing ANTIGONE]
s: Haemon is identified as Creon’s son and Antigone’s plighted bridegroom. The Chorus announces that Haemon is approaching in an angry mood, apparently distressed over Antigone or their marriage.

l: Chorus, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter GUARD bringing ANTIGONE]
s: The Chorus observes the conflict between Creon, Antigone, and Ismene and reports that Antigone’s death-warrant appears sealed. It sings of the inherited suffering of the Labdacidae and the power of Zeus, Fate, and divine punishment. It then announces Haemon’s angry arrival.

l: Polyneices, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter GUARD bringing ANTIGONE]
s: Antigone has buried her dead brother despite Creon’s prohibition. She says that the slain man was her brother and that she would have grieved with reason if she had left him unburied, even though Creon regarded him as an outlaw.

l: Antigone’s burial of her brother, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter GUARD bringing ANTIGONE]
s: Antigone’s burial consists of gathering dry dust and pouring a lustral stream from a brazen urn three times over the dead. The Guard witnesses the act after the body has been uncovered and arrests her.

l: the arrest of Antigone, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter GUARD bringing ANTIGONE]
s: The guards arrest Antigone when they see her performing burial rites over the corpse. The Guard brings her directly to Creon and identifies her as having been caught in the act.

l: Creon’s interdict, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter GUARD bringing ANTIGONE]
s: Creon’s interdict forbids the burial of the corpse. Antigone knowingly breaks it, and Creon treats her disobedience as a crime deserving death.

l: the unwritten laws of Heaven, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter GUARD bringing ANTIGONE]
s: Antigone says that the unwritten laws of Heaven were not ordained by Zeus’s human opponents, were not made yesterday or today, and cannot be annulled by a mortal ruler. She claims that these laws required her to bury her brother and justified disobeying Creon’s interdict.

l: death and mortality, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter GUARD bringing ANTIGONE]
s: Antigone accepts that she must die and says that death is a gain for someone whose life is full of misery. Creon makes death the penalty for her burial, while the Chorus presents the suffering of the Labdacidae as a continuing punishment across generations.

l: Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter HAEMON]
s: Haemon confronts Creon, urging him to listen to the people and yield to wiser counsel, but Creon refuses and orders Antigone to die. Haemon declares that Antigone’s death will bring another death and leaves in anger. Antigone is taken away to be sealed alive in a rock-hewn tomb, where she mourns her lost marriage, family, and future. The Chorus recalls others whom fate and divine power overcame, while questioning Antigone’s defiance of authority.

l: Creon, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter HAEMON]
s: Creon insists that rulers must be obeyed and that the State cannot tolerate rebellion. He rejects Haemon’s advice, orders Antigone to be sealed alive in a rock-hewn tomb, and remains convinced that he is guiltless of her blood.

l: Haemon, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter HAEMON]
s: Haemon tells Creon that the people mourn Antigone and that wisdom requires listening to others and yielding when necessary. He argues that a State ruled by one man is no State at all, warns that Antigone’s death will bring another death, and leaves after breaking with Creon.

l: Antigone, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter HAEMON]
s: Antigone bids farewell to her country and laments that she is being taken to a living tomb as an unwed bride. She defends her burial of Polyneices as an act required by conscience and mourns her father, mother, brother, marriage, and future.

l: Chorus, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter HAEMON]
s: The Chorus initially finds Creon’s words reasonable but later urges both Creon and Haemon to heed one another. It reflects on love, fate, Antigone’s suffering, and the dangers of defying authority, recalling other figures overcome by divine or destined power.

l: Thebes, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter HAEMON]
s: Thebes is invoked by Antigone as her fatherland and as the city from which her royal family sprang. The Chorus also refers to Theban chariots and the gods of Thebes.

l: the gods, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter HAEMON]
s: The gods are associated with reason, divine law, and the powers that mortals must honor. Antigone hopes that the gods will judge whether her piety or Creon’s actions are just.

l: divine justice, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter HAEMON]
s: Justice is presented as something that stands above human authority, although the Chorus says that Antigone has boldly set herself against it. The Chorus also imagines Love enthroned with Justice and bending human beings to its will.

l: the State, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter HAEMON]
s: The State is invoked by Creon as the authority that must be defended through obedience and discipline. Haemon argues that a State ruled for one man alone is no State at all.

l: the law, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter HAEMON]
s: The law is used by Creon to justify Antigone’s punishment for rebellion and by Antigone to explain her duty to honor her dead brother. Antigone says that the law of conscience led her to bury Polyneices.

l: piety, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter HAEMON]
s: Antigone identifies her actions as piety toward the dead, but says that her piety has been judged impious. She hopes that divine judgment will distinguish her reverence from the wrongs done to her.

l: Antigone’s burial of her brother, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter HAEMON]
s: Antigone says that she buried and performed the proper rites for Polyneices after he was left unsepulchered. She maintains that she would have done the same for a dead child or husband, but that Polyneices was her only possible brother because her parents were dead.

l: Antigone’s condemnation, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter HAEMON]
s: Antigone has been condemned by Creon for honoring Polyneices against the State’s command. She is treated as a criminal and sentenced to lose marriage, motherhood, companionship, and life among the living.

l: Antigone’s execution, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter HAEMON]
s: Antigone’s death is ordered by Creon, though it is to occur through being sealed alive rather than by immediate execution. Haemon declares that her death will be accompanied by another death.

l: Antigone’s burial alive, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter HAEMON]
s: Creon orders Antigone to be taken to a deserted place and sealed alive in a rock-hewn cave. She is to receive only enough food to prevent the State from bearing the taint of homicide, and may either die there or live in solitude.

l: Haemon’s confrontation with Creon, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter HAEMON]
s: Haemon confronts Creon over Antigone’s sentence, reporting that the people consider her noble rather than lawless. Their dispute expands into an argument about wisdom, popular judgment, the State, divine rights, and Creon’s authority.

l: Haemon’s departure, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter HAEMON]
s: After Creon orders Antigone’s death, Haemon says that Creon will never see his face again and exits in anger. The Chorus describes his departure as the wrath of youth under provocation.

l: Antigone’s marriage, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter HAEMON]
s: Antigone says that she goes to death as an unwed wife because no marriage song, bridal bed, or marriage joys were granted to her. She calls the tomb both her grave and her bridal chamber.

l: the cave tomb, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter HAEMON]
s: The cave tomb is a rock-hewn, isolated place where Antigone is to be walled up and left alone. Creon describes it as a dwelling in which she may die or live in solitude.

l: the tomb of Antigone, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter HAEMON]
s: Antigone calls the tomb her grave, bridal bower, prison house, and everlasting home. She expects to join her dead family there, while the Chorus later compares her fate with others confined or overcome by destiny.

l: Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter TEIRESIAS and BOY]
s: Teiresias warns Creon that the gods reject Thebes because Polyneices remains unburied, and he prophesies that Creon will suffer the loss of his own child. Creon initially accuses Teiresias and other advisers of seeking money, but after the Chorus urges him to yield, he goes to free Antigone and bury Polyneices. Creon reaches Antigone’s tomb too late: Antigone is dead, and Haemon kills himself beside her after attacking his father. Eurydice then kills herself, cursing Creon, who recognizes his guilt and is left crushed by grief and Fate.

l: Teiresias, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter TEIRESIAS and BOY]
s: Teiresias comes with a boy as his guide and warns Creon that the gods reject the city because Polyneices remains unburied. After Creon accuses him of prophecy for profit, Teiresias foretells that Creon will pay with the life of his own child and that lamentation will fill his halls.

l: Creon, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter TEIRESIAS and BOY]
s: Creon rejects Teiresias’s warning and accuses prophets of greed, but he eventually accepts the Chorus’s advice to free Antigone and bury Polyneices. He arrives too late to prevent Haemon’s death, then learns of Eurydice’s suicide and acknowledges that his own decisions caused the deaths.

l: Chorus, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter TEIRESIAS and BOY]
s: The Chorus confirms that Teiresias’s warnings have never failed and urges Creon to free Antigone and bury Polyneices immediately. It later declares that wisdom is the chief part of happiness and that mortals who defraud the gods face danger and punishment.

l: Eurydice, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter TEIRESIAS and BOY]
s: Eurydice hears the report of Haemon’s death and asks the first Messenger to tell her what happened. She later kills herself beside an altar after mourning Megareus and Haemon, and with her last breath curses Creon as the slayer of her child.

l: the first Messenger, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter TEIRESIAS and BOY]
s: The first Messenger reports that Haemon was found holding Antigone’s dead body in the tomb. He explains that Haemon attacked Creon, missed, and then fell on his own sword, dying while clasping Antigone.

l: Haemon, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter TEIRESIAS and BOY]
s: Haemon is found in Antigone’s tomb beside her strangled body. He attacks Creon with a sword, misses, and then kills himself with the sword, dying while embracing Antigone.

l: Antigone, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter TEIRESIAS and BOY]
s: Antigone is found dead inside the rocky tomb, strangled by a linen noose. Haemon dies beside her, and the first Messenger describes their deaths as marriage rites consummated in the halls of Death.

l: Polyneices, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter TEIRESIAS and BOY]
s: Polyneices’s corpse has been gnawed and mauled by animals and remains exposed. After Teiresias’s warning, Creon orders that the body be washed, placed on branches, burned, and covered with a mound of earth.

l: Thebes, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter TEIRESIAS and BOY]
s: Thebes is said to be polluted because the flesh of Polyneices has filled the maws of dogs and crows. The Chorus calls on Dionysus to save the city from its present distress.

l: Fate, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter TEIRESIAS and BOY]
s: Creon recognizes that Fate is difficult to resist and that his attempt to fight it has brought ruin. At the end, he feels the crushing weight of Fate and asks to be taken away.

l: the gods, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter TEIRESIAS and BOY]
s: The gods are angered because Polyneices remains unburied and because Antigone has been entombed alive. Their vengeance is described as swift against the impenitent, and the Chorus says that mortals cannot find refuge from the doom of Fate.

l: the tomb of Antigone, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter TEIRESIAS and BOY]
s: The tomb is described as a caverned rock and the bridal chamber of the maid and Death. Antigone is found dead inside it, with Haemon dying beside her.

l: the unburied body of Polyneices, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter TEIRESIAS and BOY]
s: The unburied body of Polyneices has been mauled and partly consumed by animals, causing the gods to reject prayers and offerings. Creon eventually has it washed, burned, and covered with earth.

l: the prophecy of Teiresias, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter TEIRESIAS and BOY]
s: Teiresias’s prophecy says that Creon will give the life of his own child in payment for entombing Antigone alive and leaving Polyneices unburied. It is fulfilled through Haemon’s death and is followed by further lamentation in Creon’s house.

l: the burial of Polyneices, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter TEIRESIAS and BOY]
s: Creon initially refuses to allow Polyneices’s burial, even in the face of divine signs. After Teiresias’s warning, he orders his men to bury the body, and the first Messenger reports that the burial rites have been performed.

l: Haemon's death, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter TEIRESIAS and BOY]
s: Haemon’s death occurs in Antigone’s tomb after he finds her dead. He attacks Creon, misses, and then drives a sword through his own side, dying while holding Antigone.

l: Eurydice's suicide, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter TEIRESIAS and BOY]
s: Eurydice kills herself beside an altar with a sharp sword after hearing of Haemon’s death. Before dying, she mourns Megareus and Haemon and curses Creon for their deaths.

l: Creon's guilt and punishment, Plays of Sophocles: Oedipus the King; Oedipus at Colonus; Antigone, [Enter TEIRESIAS and BOY]
s: Creon admits that he is responsible for Haemon’s and Eurydice’s deaths, calling himself their murderer. He asks to be led away and longs for death, while the Chorus says that he must endure the consequences and that wisdom comes through chastisement.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: The Introduction explains why Greek, Roman, and Scandinavian mythology is studied and describes the peoples, languages, and imaginative traditions associated with them. It outlines the Greek conception of the earth, the River Ocean, the realms of the blessed, and Mount Olympus, the home of the gods. It then relates the succession of Uranus, Kronos, and Jupiter and describes the principal Greek and Roman deities, their powers, families, symbols, and stories. The unit also introduces various lesser deities, including the Muses, Fates, Furies, Nemesis, Pan, Satyrs, Momus, and Plutus.

l: Introduction, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: The Introduction states that the book teaches enough Greek, Roman, and Scandinavian mythology to make literary allusions intelligible. It explains the mythological structure of the universe and introduces the principal gods and goddesses.

l: Greeks, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: The Greeks and Romans are described as belonging to the Aryan family of mankind. Greek writers were more playful and imaginative than the Romans and supplied most of the stories of ancient mythology.

l: Romans, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: The Romans are described as practical rather than poetical or imaginative, and as inventing few stories about their gods. They worshipped ancestors, maintained family rites around the hearth, and later incorporated Greek legends and identified Greek gods with their own deities.

l: Greek mythology, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: Greek mythology contains stories shaped by Greek imagination and by legends borrowed from Egypt and the East. The same myth may occur in several different forms in Greek and Roman authors.

l: Aryan family of mankind, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: The Aryan family of mankind is described as the race or stock to which the Greeks and Romans belonged. Its tribes were said to have emigrated from the high tablelands of Northern India, leaving traces of their language in many regions.

l: Greek poets, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: The Greek poets conceived the earth as flat and circular, with their own country near its center. They also imagined Mount Olympus as the abode of the gods and described the surrounding regions and divine realms.

l: Earth, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: The earth was believed to be a flat, circular disk divided into two equal parts by the Mediterranean Sea and the Euxine. The River Ocean was thought to flow around it.

l: Olympus, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: Mount Olympus, in Thessaly, was regarded as the abode of the gods and sometimes as the central point of the earth. Its summit contained the palace and separate dwellings of the Olympian gods.

l: Mediterranean Sea, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: The Mediterranean Sea, together with its continuation the Euxine, was called the Sea by the Greeks. It crossed the circular disk of the earth from west to east and divided it into two equal parts.

l: River Ocean, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: The River Ocean flowed around the earth in a steady current, from south to north on the western side and in the opposite direction on the eastern side. The sea and all earthly rivers were believed to receive their waters from it.

l: Hyperboreans, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: The Hyperboreans were imagined as a happy people living beyond the north wind in an everlasting spring. They were exempt from disease, old age, toil, and warfare, and their country was inaccessible by land or sea.

l: the Aethiopians, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: The AEthiopians were said to live near the River Ocean on the southern side of the earth. They were happy and virtuous, and the gods sometimes left Olympus to share their sacrifices and banquets.

l: the Elysian fields, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: The Elysian Plain lay on the western margin of the earth by the River Ocean. Mortals favored by the gods were transported there without dying and enjoyed immortal bliss; it was also called the fortunate fields and the Isles of the Blessed.

l: Olympian gods, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: The Olympian gods lived on Mount Olympus, where they had separate dwellings and assembled in Jupiter's palace when summoned. They feasted on ambrosia and nectar, listened to Apollo and the Muses, and retired to sleep in their own dwellings at night.

l: Jupiter, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: Jupiter, or Zeus, was the real monarch of heaven and the father of gods and men. He was the son of Saturn and Ops, defeated Saturn and the Titans, ruled the heavens, wielded the thunder, and carried the shield called the Aegis; the eagle was his favorite bird.

l: Apollo, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: Apollo, or Phoebus Apollo, was the son of Jupiter and Latona and the brother of Diana. He was the god of archery, prophecy, music, and the sun, and he delighted the gods by playing the lyre.

l: Muses, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: The Muses were nine daughters of Jupiter and Mnemosyne, or Memory. They presided over song and memory, with each assigned to a department of literature, art, or science.

l: Kronos, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: Kronos was the Greek counterpart of Saturn and belonged to the race of Titans. He was born from Uranus, overthrew Uranus, was later defeated by Jupiter, and was sometimes confused with Chronos, or Time.

l: Vulcan, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: Vulcan, or Hephaistos, was the celestial artist and the son of Jupiter and Juno. He was lame, was thrown from heaven to Lemnos, and forged Jupiter's thunderbolts.

l: Mars, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: Mars, or Ares, was the god of war and the son of Jupiter and Juno.

l: Neptune, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: Neptune, or Poseidon, was the brother of Jupiter and Pluto. After Saturn's dethronement, Neptune received dominion over the ocean.

l: Venus, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: Venus, or Aphrodite, was the goddess of love and beauty and was said to be the daughter of Jupiter and Dione or to have sprung from sea foam. She became the wife of Vulcan, possessed the love-inspiring Cestus, and was associated with swans, doves, the rose, and the myrtle.

l: Minerva, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: Minerva, or Pallas Athene, was the goddess of wisdom and sprang fully armed from Jupiter's head without a mother. Her favorite bird was the owl, and the olive was sacred to her.

l: Diana, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: Diana, or Artemis, was the daughter of Jupiter and Latona and the sister of Apollo. She was the goddess of the moon.

l: Mercury, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: Mercury, or Hermes, was the son of Jupiter and Maia and the messenger of Jupiter. He presided over commerce, wrestling, gymnastics, thievery, and activities requiring skill and dexterity; he wore winged footwear and carried the caduceus, and he invented the lyre.

l: Uranus, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: Uranus, or Ouranos, represented Heaven embracing all things. He was described as the source from which Kronos or Saturn was born.

l: Titans, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: The Titans were the children of Earth and Heaven and included Saturn, Rhea, Oceanus, Hyperion, Iapetus, Ophion, Themis, Mnemosyne, and Eurynome. Jupiter defeated them, imprisoned some in Tartarus, and imposed other penalties on others, including condemning Atlas to bear the heavens.

l: Chaos, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: Chaos was described as the origin from which Earth and Heaven sprang in one account of the universe. Another account placed Earth, Erebus, and Love among the first beings.

l: Juno, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: Juno, or Hera, was the wife of Jupiter and queen of the gods. Iris attended and served as her messenger, and the peacock was her favorite bird.

l: Cupid, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: Cupid, or Eros, was the son and constant companion of Venus. Armed with a bow and arrows, he shot the darts of desire into gods and mortals; he grew rapidly after Anteros was born.

l: Ceres, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: Ceres, or Demeter, was the daughter of Saturn and Rhea and the mother of Proserpine. She presided over agriculture.

l: Proserpine, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: Proserpine, or Persephone, was the daughter of Ceres. She became the wife of Pluto and queen of the realms of the dead.

l: Pluto, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: Pluto, or Dis, was the brother of Jupiter and Neptune. When Saturn's dominions were divided, Pluto received the realms of the dead.

l: Bacchus, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: Bacchus, or Dionysus, was the son of Jupiter and Semele and the god of wine. He represented wine's intoxicating, social, and beneficent influences and was regarded as a promoter of civilization, a lawgiver, and a lover of peace.

l: creation of the universe, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: One account of the creation says that Chaos produced Earth and Heaven, from whom the Titans descended. Another says that Earth, Erebus, and Love were first, with Love issuing from the egg of Night that floated on Chaos and bringing life and joy through his arrows and torch.

l: Jupiter's division of Saturn's dominions, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter I
s: After Jupiter and his brothers defeated Saturn, Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto divided Saturn's dominions. Jupiter received the heavens, Neptune the ocean, and Pluto the realms of the dead, while Earth and Olympus remained common property.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, ROMAN DIVINITIES
s: This unit describes Roman divinities and identifies several as peculiar to Roman mythology, while noting that some Grecian divinities were also received by the Romans. It explains Saturn's reign during the Golden Age, the Saturnalia held in his memory, and the roles of deities including Vesta, Janus, and others. It also distinguishes the household gods Penates and Lares and describes the protective spirits called Genius and Juno. The unit concludes with a passage by Macaulay and notes on the pronunciation of proper names.

l: Roman divinities, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, ROMAN DIVINITIES
s: Roman divinities described in this unit include gods and goddesses associated with agriculture, war, boundaries, childbirth, hearths, gates, households, and personal protection. Some are identified as peculiar to Roman mythology, while others have names or counterparts connected with Grecian divinities.

l: Roman mythology, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, ROMAN DIVINITIES
s: Roman mythology includes Saturn, Faunus, Quirinus, Bellona, Terminus, Pales, Pomona, Flora, Lucina, Vesta, Janus, the Penates, the Lares, Genius, and Juno. Roman poets identified Saturn with the Grecian god Kronos and connected Vesta with the Grecian Hestia.

l: Saturn, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, ROMAN DIVINITIES
s: Saturn was an ancient Italian deity whom Roman poets identified with the Grecian god Kronos. After Jupiter dethroned him, he was said to have fled to Italy, where he reigned during the Golden Age.

l: Golden Age, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, ROMAN DIVINITIES
s: The Golden Age was the period during which Saturn was said to have reigned in Italy after fleeing there following his dethronement by Jupiter.

l: Saturnalia, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, ROMAN DIVINITIES
s: Saturnalia was held every year in winter in memory of Saturn's beneficent dominion. Public business was suspended, declarations of war and criminal executions were postponed, friends exchanged presents, and slaves were given great liberties, including a feast at which their masters served them.

l: Vesta, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, ROMAN DIVINITIES
s: Vesta, identified with the Grecian Hestia, presided over the public and private hearth. A sacred fire burned in her temple under the care of six virgin priestesses called Vestals; if the fire went out through their neglect, they were severely punished, and it was rekindled from the rays of the sun.

l: Janus, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, ROMAN DIVINITIES
s: Janus was the porter of heaven, the guardian deity of gates, and the deity who opened the year, with the first month named after him. He was commonly represented with two heads because every door looks two ways; in Rome, the gates of his principal temple were open in war and closed in peace, though they were shut only once between the reign of Numa and that of Augustus.

l: Rome, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, ROMAN DIVINITIES
s: Rome had numerous temples of Janus. Its public safety was held to be connected with the preservation of Vesta's sacred fire.

l: Penates, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, ROMAN DIVINITIES
s: The Penates were household gods believed to attend to the welfare and prosperity of the family. Their name came from Penus, the pantry, which was sacred to them, and each master of a family served as priest to the Penates of his own house.

l: Lares, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, ROMAN DIVINITIES
s: The Lares, or Lars, were household gods regarded as the deified spirits of mortals. The family Lars were believed to be the souls of ancestors who watched over and protected their descendants.

l: Genius, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, ROMAN DIVINITIES
s: The Romans believed that every man had a Genius, a spirit who had given him being and protected him throughout life. Men made offerings to their Genius on their birthdays.

l: Juno, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, ROMAN DIVINITIES
s: The Romans believed that every woman had her Juno, a spirit who had given her being and protected her throughout life. Women made offerings to their Juno on their birthdays.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, CHAPTER II
s: Ovid's creation narrative describes how God and Nature separated Chaos into earth, sea, air, and heaven, and how man was made in the image of the gods. Prometheus gave man fire, while Pandora's opening of a jar released evils but left hope behind. After humanity declined from the Golden Age into violence and corruption, Jupiter destroyed the world with a flood, sparing only Deucalion and Pyrrha on Mount Parnassus. They followed an oracle's command to cast stones behind them, from which a new human race arose, while Prometheus was later imprisoned and tortured for aiding mankind.

l: Ovid, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, CHAPTER II
s: Ovid gives a connected narrative of creation, the decline of the human ages, the flood, and the renewal of mankind.

l: Earth, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, CHAPTER II
s: The earth was separated from the sea and heaven, sank below the air, and was organized with rivers, bays, mountains, valleys, woods, fields, and plains. It later became divided into private possessions and was overwhelmed by Jupiter's flood.

l: the sea, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, CHAPTER II
s: The sea was separated from the earth and heaven and placed in the lowest position, buoying up the earth. Jupiter and Neptune later caused it to cover the land during the flood before it returned to its shores.

l: Uranus, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, CHAPTER II
s: Heaven was separated from the earth and sea, with its fiery portion rising to form the skies. The gods' palaces were said to stand along the Milky Way in heaven.

l: human race, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, CHAPTER II
s: Man was made in the image of the gods with an upright stature and was given fire by Prometheus. Fire enabled man to make weapons and tools, cultivate the earth, warm his dwelling, and resist the cold; later, mankind became violent and corrupt before being destroyed by the flood.

l: Prometheus, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, CHAPTER II
s: Prometheus, a Titan and son of Iapetus and Themis, helped make man and brought fire from heaven with Minerva's aid after Epimetheus had given other animals their gifts. He taught and protected mankind, but Jupiter condemned him to perpetual imprisonment on Mount Caucasus, where a vulture preyed on his liver. Prometheus refused to reveal the fatal marriage that would bring about Jupiter's ruin and became a symbol of endurance and resistance to oppression.

l: Epimetheus, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, CHAPTER II
s: Epimetheus was charged with making animals and giving them faculties such as courage, strength, swiftness, sagacity, wings, claws, and shells. He used all his gifts before reaching man, accepted Pandora despite Prometheus's warning, and was connected with the jar kept in his house.

l: fire, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, CHAPTER II
s: Prometheus lit his torch at the chariot of the sun and brought fire down to man. Fire gave man power to make weapons and tools, cultivate the earth, warm his dwelling, and defy the cold.

l: Jupiter, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, CHAPTER II
s: Jupiter sent Pandora to punish Prometheus, Epimetheus, and man for the theft and acceptance of fire. Angered by human corruption, he decided to destroy mankind, changed his plan from burning the world to drowning it, and summoned Neptune's aid. He later spared Deucalion and Pyrrha after seeing their harmless and pious lives.

l: Pandora, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, CHAPTER II
s: Pandora was made in heaven with gifts from the gods, including beauty from Venus, persuasion from Mercury, and music from Apollo. She was sent to earth and accepted by Epimetheus, then opened a container out of curiosity, releasing either plagues or blessings while hope remained inside.

l: gods, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, CHAPTER II
s: The gods contributed gifts to perfect Pandora and lived in palaces along the Milky Way, while the common people of the skies lived apart. They were summoned by Jupiter to hear his plan to destroy the corrupt human race, and they gradually abandoned the earth as violence spread.

l: Pandora's jar, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, CHAPTER II
s: Pandora's jar was kept in Epimetheus's house and contained noxious articles that had not been needed when man was fitted for his new abode. When Pandora removed its cover, bodily and mental evils escaped and scattered, leaving hope as the only remaining thing inside.

l: hope, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, CHAPTER II
s: Hope was the one thing left in Pandora's jar after the evils escaped. The narrative says that hope never entirely leaves mankind and can prevent people from becoming completely wretched.

l: Golden Age, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, CHAPTER II
s: The Golden Age was the first age of humanity, marked by innocence, happiness, truth, and right without laws or magistrates. The earth supplied necessities without labor, perpetual spring prevailed, and rivers flowed with milk and wine while honey came from the oaks.

l: flood, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, CHAPTER II
s: Jupiter's flood covered the earth after Notus darkened the sky, torrents fell, rivers overflowed, the ocean advanced, and an earthquake heaved the land. People, animals, houses, temples, and crops were swept away, leaving only a few survivors and Parnassus above the waves.

l: Parnassus, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, CHAPTER II
s: Parnassus was the only mountain said to overtop the floodwaters. Deucalion and Pyrrha found refuge there.

l: Deucalion, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, CHAPTER II
s: Deucalion, a just man of the race of Prometheus, survived the flood with Pyrrha on Parnassus. He sought guidance from the gods, interpreted the oracle's reference to the bones of their mother as stones from the earth, and cast them behind him to renew mankind.

l: Pyrrha, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, CHAPTER II
s: Pyrrha, a faithful worshipper of the gods, survived the flood with Deucalion. She initially feared that the oracle's command to cast behind them the bones of their mother meant profaning their parents' remains, but followed Deucalion's interpretation and cast stones that became women.

l: oracle, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, CHAPTER II
s: The oracle instructed Deucalion and Pyrrha to leave the temple with veiled heads and unbound garments and cast behind them the bones of their mother. Deucalion interpreted the command to mean that they should cast stones, the bones of the earth.

l: stones, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, CHAPTER II
s: The stones cast behind Deucalion and Pyrrha softened and took on human form. Those thrown by Deucalion became men, and those thrown by Pyrrha became women, forming a hard race suited to labor.

l: Titan, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, CHAPTER II
s: Prometheus is identified as a Titan who favored mankind and gave it knowledge, arts, and protection. Because he aided humanity and defied Jupiter, he was bound to a rock on Mount Caucasus and tormented by a vulture.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, PYTHON
s: The unit recounts Apollo's slaying of Python, the founding of the Pythian games and the Delphic oracle, and Apollo's unsuccessful pursuit of Daphne, who becomes a laurel tree. It then tells how Pyramus and Thisbe's forbidden love ends in their deaths beneath a white mulberry tree, whose berries become purple. Finally, it relates Cephalus's mistaken killing of Procris with her own javelin after she suspects him of loving the breeze.

l: Python, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, PYTHON
s: Python was an enormous serpent that arose from the slime left by the flood and terrorized the people while hiding in the caves of Mount Parnassus. Apollo slew Python with his arrows.

l: Apollo, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, PYTHON
s: Apollo slew Python and founded the Pythian games and his oracle at Delphi. He pursued Daphne after Cupid caused him to fall in love with her, and he later claimed the laurel as his tree. He was also described as the god of music, poetry, medicine, song, and the lyre.

l: Pythian games, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, PYTHON
s: Apollo instituted the Pythian games to commemorate his victory over Python. Victors in feats of strength, foot races, or chariot races were crowned with wreaths of beech leaves because the laurel had not yet become Apollo's tree.

l: Delphic oracle, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, PYTHON
s: Apollo founded the Delphic oracle, which was consulted by many nations and held in high repute throughout the world. Its decrees were followed when the laws of Lycurgus were introduced and the earliest Greek colonies were founded, and cities and other enterprises commonly sought its advice.

l: Delphi, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, PYTHON
s: Delphi was the place where Apollo founded his oracle. Apollo also called himself lord of Delphos while pursuing Daphne.

l: Apollo and Daphne, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, PYTHON
s: Apollo and Daphne are the subjects of a story in which Cupid makes Apollo love Daphne while making Daphne reject love. Apollo pursues her until she is transformed into a laurel tree, which he adopts as his own tree.

l: Cupid, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, PYTHON
s: Cupid became angry when Apollo mocked his bow and arrows. He used a golden arrow to make Apollo love Daphne and a leaden arrow to make Daphne reject love.

l: Daphne, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, PYTHON
s: Daphne was the daughter of the river god Peneus and preferred woodland sports and hunting to marriage. After Cupid caused her to reject love, she fled Apollo and prayed for escape, whereupon she was transformed into a laurel tree.

l: Peneus, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, PYTHON
s: Peneus was the river god and Daphne's father. When Apollo pursued Daphne, she called upon Peneus to open the earth or change her form, and she was changed into a tree.

l: laurel tree, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, PYTHON
s: The laurel tree was Daphne's transformed form. Apollo declared that he would wear it as his crown and use it to decorate his harp and quiver, and that it would remain eternally green without decay.

l: Pyramus and Thisbe, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, PYTHON
s: Pyramus and Thisbe were young lovers in Babylonia whose parents forbade them to marry. A misunderstanding involving a lioness led Pyramus and then Thisbe to kill themselves, and they were buried together while the mulberry tree preserved the memory of their blood.

l: Pyramus, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, PYTHON
s: Pyramus was described as the handsomest youth in Babylonia and loved Thisbe despite their parents' opposition. Believing that a lioness had killed Thisbe after finding her bloody veil, he stabbed himself beneath the appointed tree.

l: Thisbe, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, PYTHON
s: Thisbe was described as the fairest maiden in Babylonia and loved Pyramus. She fled from a lioness and lost her veil, then killed herself with Pyramus's sword after finding him dying.

l: the tomb of Ninus, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, PYTHON
s: The tomb of Ninus was the agreed meeting place outside the city's bounds where Pyramus and Thisbe planned to meet secretly. Thisbe went there first and waited beneath the appointed tree.

l: white mulberry tree, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, PYTHON
s: The white mulberry tree stood near a cool spring beside the tomb of Ninus. Pyramus's blood stained its white berries red, and after the lovers' deaths it bore purple berries as a memorial.

l: lioness, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, PYTHON
s: The lioness approached the spring with blood on its jaws after a recent slaughter. It frightened Thisbe away and tore her discarded veil with its bloody mouth, causing Pyramus to believe that she had been killed.

l: Thisbe's veil, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, PYTHON
s: Thisbe's veil fell as she fled from the lioness. The lioness tore and bloodied it, and Pyramus found it and mistook it as proof of Thisbe's death.

l: Pyramus's sword, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, PYTHON
s: Pyramus's sword was used by Pyramus to stab himself after he believed Thisbe dead. Thisbe later used the same sword to kill herself.

l: Cephalus and Procris, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, PYTHON
s: Cephalus and Procris were devoted spouses whose relationship was destroyed by suspicion and misunderstanding. Procris hid to investigate Cephalus's words about the breeze, and Cephalus accidentally killed her with a javelin.

l: Cephalus, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, PYTHON
s: Cephalus was a beautiful youth devoted to hunting and to his wife, Procris. After mistaking Procris's movement in the bushes for a wild animal, he threw the javelin she had given him and fatally wounded her.

l: Procris, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, PYTHON
s: Procris was Cephalus's wife, a favorite of Diana, and the giver of his unfailing javelin and swift dog. Suspecting that Cephalus loved another, she hid while he spoke to the breeze; he then accidentally struck and killed her with her own gift.

l: Aurora, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, PYTHON
s: Aurora saw Cephalus at dawn, fell in love with him, and carried him away. When he resisted her because he loved Procris, she warned that he would eventually regret having his wife.

l: Lelaps, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, PYTHON
s: Lelaps was Cephalus's dog, given to Procris by Diana and then given by Procris to Cephalus. It could outrun every rival, but when it chased the fox, both animals were turned to stone because the heavenly powers would not allow either to win.

l: the fox, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, PYTHON
s: The fox was sent by an angry deity to ravage the country and could not be caught by ordinary dogs. Lelaps chased it in vain until both the fox and the dog were suddenly transformed into stone.

l: Procris's javelin, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, PYTHON
s: Procris's javelin was a weapon that never failed to hit its mark and was given to Procris by Diana. Procris gave it to Cephalus, who later threw it at the bushes and accidentally killed her.

l: the breeze, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, PYTHON
s: The breeze was the subject of Cephalus's affectionate calls while he rested after hunting. Procris misunderstood those calls as evidence that Cephalus loved another, and her suspicion led to the encounter in which she was killed.

l: Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter III
s: Jupiter changes Io into a heifer to conceal his affair, but Juno has Argus guard her until Mercury kills him and Jupiter persuades Juno to restore Io. Juno changes Callisto into a bear, but Jupiter places Callisto and her son Arcas in the heavens as the Great and Little Bear. Diana changes Actaeon into a stag after he sees her bathing, and his own hunting dogs pursue and kill him.
