The unit also explains the origins of the Syrinx pipes and describes the constellations, including the Little Bear and the Pole star.

l: Jupiter, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter III
s: Jupiter changes Io into a heifer when Juno approaches, gives her to Juno when refusing would arouse suspicion, and later sends Mercury to kill Argus. He intercedes for Io and promises Juno that he will not pay her any more attentions, leading Juno to restore Io's human form. Jupiter also rescues Callisto and her son from death and places them in the heavens as the Great and Little Bear.

l: Juno, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter III
s: Juno suspects Jupiter of unfaithfulness, discovers Io in the form of a heifer, and gives her to Argus to watch. After Mercury kills Argus, Juno places his eyes on the tail of her peacock and sends a gadfly to torment Io. Juno changes Callisto into a bear and later persuades Tethys and Oceanus to forbid the Great and Little Bear from entering their waters.

l: Io, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter III
s: Io, the daughter of Inachus, is changed into a heifer by Jupiter and guarded by Argus. She reveals her identity to her father by writing her name in the sand with her hoof, then flees across the world from Juno's gadfly. Jupiter's intercession leads Juno to restore Io's human form, and she is returned to her father and sisters.

l: Argus, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter III
s: Argus has a hundred eyes and keeps constant watch over Io, sleeping with no more than two eyes at a time. Mercury disguises himself as a shepherd, lulls Argus to sleep with stories and music, and cuts through his neck. Juno places Argus's eyes as ornaments on her peacock's tail.

l: Mercury, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter III
s: Mercury goes to earth at Jupiter's command to dispatch Argus. Disguised as a shepherd, he plays the Syrinx pipes, tells stories, and finally kills Argus when all of Argus's eyes are asleep.

l: Syrinx, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter III
s: Syrinx is a nymph who rejects the satyrs and spirits of the wood and remains a faithful worshipper of Diana. When Pan pursues her, the water nymphs change her into reeds. The sound of Pan's sigh through the reeds inspires the instrument called Syrinx.

l: Pan, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter III
s: Pan pursues Syrinx after meeting her, but embraces only reeds when the water nymphs transform her. He makes an instrument from reeds of unequal lengths and calls it Syrinx in her honor.

l: Callisto, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter III
s: Callisto excites Juno's jealousy, and Juno changes her into a bear. Though her form changes, her former disposition remains, and she wanders fearfully through the woods. Callisto recognizes her grown son while hunting, but Jupiter saves them both and places them in the heavens as the Great and Little Bear.

l: Arcas, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter III
s: Arcas is Callisto's son, whom she recognizes as a young man while he is hunting. He nearly kills his transformed mother, but Jupiter rescues both of them and places them in the heavens. The text identifies him as the source of the name 'Star of Aready,' because he and Callisto lived in Arcadia.

l: Little Bear, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter III
s: The Little Bear is one of the two constellations formed when Jupiter places Callisto and Arcas in the heavens. It moves around the heavens but never sinks beneath the ocean because of Juno's request to Tethys and Oceanus. The last star in its tail is the Pole star, also called the Cynosure.

l: Pole star, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter III
s: The Pole star is the last star in the tail of the Little Bear and is also called the Cynosure. The text describes it as a guide of mariners and associates it with the magnetic attraction of the North.

l: Diana, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter III
s: Diana is the huntress-queen and goddess of the woods. While bathing with her nymphs, she is seen by Actaeon, so she changes him into a stag and causes his own dogs to pursue and kill him.

l: Actaeon, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter III
s: Actaeon, the son of King Cadmus, is hunting when he wanders into the place where Diana is bathing. Diana changes him into a stag, leaving his consciousness intact but taking away his human voice and form. His own hunting dogs and fellow-huntsmen pursue him, and the dogs tear him to death.
